title_en: Proposed triennial PFOS/PFOA tests for specified buildings using non-waterworks water (2026)

quick_take.what_changed: MHLW proposed PFOS/PFOA testing once every three years in specified buildings drawing some or all drinking water from sources other than waterworks or dedicated waterworks, such as groundwater. Consultation closed on 16 October 2026; promulgation of this proposal has not been confirmed.
quick_take.who_is_affected: Owners and managers of specified buildings using groundwater or other non-waterworks sources, building-sanitation management firms and testing laboratories; not all specified buildings have the same proposed testing duty.
quick_take.what_to_do_now: Continue complying with existing building drinking-water and maintenance standards, identify PFOS/PFOA sampling needs and monitor the finalized regulation; do not claim the proposed triennial test is already in force.

instruments.number: 昭和四十六年厚生省令第二号
instruments.name_ja: 建築物における衛生的環境の確保に関する法律施行規則
instruments.name_en: Enforcement Regulations under the Act on Maintenance of Sanitation in Buildings (existing ordinance proposed for amendment)

paragraphs: The Building Sanitation Act already requires persons with authority over specified buildings to maintain a sanitary environment, including supplying drinking and other relevant water that meets applicable standards when facilities provide water for human consumption. The Enforcement Regulations set inspection items by reference to the water-quality standards. A change to the drinking-water standards may leave a mismatch if the building-specific inspection list is not updated consistently.

Japan treated perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS) and perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), persistent organic fluorine compounds, as water-quality management targets before placing the combined concentration under a binding drinking-water standard. The Environment Ministry's June 2025 amendment introduced a combined 50 ng/L standard, effective from 1 April 2026, after scientific review and consultation. That established obligation for regulated water suppliers is different from the additional building-specific periodic-inspection proposal.

The September 2026 MHLW proposal would amend Article 4(1)(iv)(d) of the Building Sanitation Act Enforcement Regulations to add PFOS and PFOA to the triennial test category. This category applies where all or part of the drinking-water supply comes from sources other than waterworks or dedicated waterworks, such as groundwater. In contrast, buildings drawing water only from waterworks or dedicated waterworks have a different inspection category and regulated supply-chain controls. The proposal seeks to close the building-level testing gap for non-waterworks water; it does not impose the proposed triennial test on every residence or every specified building.

Japan's building-sanitation regime and water-supply regulation pursue related but legally distinct goals: protection of water quality at the supplier stage and hygienic maintenance within covered buildings. Earlier PFOS/PFOA management used provisional targets; after the Food Safety Commission's 2024 health-risk assessment and environmental regulatory deliberations, the Environment Ministry promulgated a revised drinking-water standard on 30 June 2025, effective 1 April 2026, with a combined 50 ng/L limit.

At the 15 September 2026 MHLW Living Environment Subcommittee meeting, officials distinguished waterworks/dedicated-waterworks supply from groundwater or other non-waterworks supply. The latter falls into the existing three-year testing category; the ministry estimated that only a few percent of the 48,608 specified buildings recorded at the end of FY2024 used this source category, based on inquiries to major local governments. On 16 September, MHLW opened e-Gov consultation 495260188 to add PFOS/PFOA to that category; consultation closed at 00:00 Japan time on 16 October 2026.

The one-page official draft summary estimated promulgation during November 2026 and commencement in May 2027, described as six months after promulgation. Those are forecasts in the consultation document, not proof of enacted commencement. The e-Gov building-sanitation ordinance revision history examined on 11 November 2026 does not yet identify this new PFOS/PFOA testing amendment as promulgated.

confirmed.text: Public consultation 495260188 closed at 00:00 Japan time; the comment period is over.

expected: MHLW may consider public submissions and finalize a ministerial ordinance. Its September draft anticipated promulgation in November 2026 and commencement in May 2027, six months after promulgation, but those dates require confirmation in the final official text.

Owners and building sanitation managers should update water-inspection plans only in accordance with the enacted scope and transitional provisions, while maintaining already-applicable hygiene and drinking-water duties.
uncertainties: The precise promulgation date, effective date, final scope, sampling methodology and transitional arrangements for specified buildings have not been established by the cited draft consultation alone.

Individual application depends both on specified-building status and whether drinking water is supplied wholly or partly from sources outside waterworks or dedicated waterworks; the triennial category must not be generalized to all buildings.
The water-supply regulation's own PFOS/PFOA inspection frequency and the proposed building-sanitation three-year inspection are separate obligations and should not be treated as interchangeable.

paragraphs: Managers of specified buildings drawing all or some drinking water from groundwater or other non-waterworks/dedicated-waterworks sources may need to add PFOS/PFOA to the once-every-three-years test schedule once the proposal is finalized. Managers relying solely on waterworks or dedicated waterworks should not automatically be described as subject to the same proposed triennial building test. Building-maintenance firms and laboratories should check the final scope, sampling, methods, scheduling, reporting and records. The draft does not itself establish a new concentration limit separate from the existing water-quality standard.

Property owners should distinguish what is binding already under the existing building-sanitation framework, what became binding on regulated water suppliers under the April 2026 drinking-water standard, and the separate proposed inspection schedule for building owners. Prematurely claiming the proposal has been implemented can generate inaccurate vendor instructions and compliance records; ignoring the existing potable-water standards can create a different compliance risk.
checklist: Identify each legally specified building and whether any drinking water comes from groundwater or other sources besides waterworks/dedicated waterworks; do not assume that every specified building is in the triennial testing category.
Retain existing required water testing and hygiene controls; plan for potential PFOS/PFOA tests once every three years but mark this as a draft requirement until promulgation.
Review the Environment Ministry's existing combined 50 ng/L drinking-water standard separately from the frequency and scope of building-level checks.
Monitor the final MHLW ordinance, commencement and transition rules, then update inspection contracts, laboratory scope and records based on the adopted provisions.
